FAST

TOKYO, Oct 8 : The Bank of Japan said on Thursday price increases driven by higher raw material costs were spreading to consumer goods with some firms hiking prices more frequently than in the past, signaling its concern over broadening inflationary pressure. The central bank also offered an upbeat view on the economic outlook, saying brisk AI-related demand was increasing domestic output for electronic goods, machinery and telecommunication infrastructure. "Many regions saw firms passing on a broad range of rising costs," including higher raw material costs from the Middle East conflict and the weak yen, as well as increasing labour costs, the BOJ said in a statement released after a quarterly meeting of its regional branch managers. The BOJ raised its economic assessment for two of the country's nine regions and maintained its view for the remaining areas, saying they were all recovering moderately. Given volatile moves in input costs, some firms are raising prices more frequently than in the past, the statement said. "Efforts to pass-through rising costs are spreading to firms close to consumers," leading to more companies raising prices, the statement said.

Source: Reuters

FAST

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, according to US officials and others familiar with the outreach, in a sharp reversal of Washington’s efforts to isolate the country’s generals after the 2021 coup. The US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, Michael Vance, played a leading role in the outreach, which has focused on shutting down scam centres that target Americans but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, according to seven current and former officials and others familiar with the policy shift. Vance joined talks with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing in the capital Naypyitaw on Sep 15 and Sep 16. The meeting was aimed at securing the release of American businessman Adam Castillo but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the people said. Last month’s meeting - the highest‑level contact since the coup - underscores a broader Trump‑administration foreign policy tilt away from democracy promotion toward transactional engagement.

The presence of Vance, who was confirmed as the State Department’s top intelligence official in August, and his ongoing role in US policy toward Myanmar have not been previously reported.

Related:

MILITARY LEADER REMAINS UNDER US SANCTIONS Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief, remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide.  Less than two weeks after Vance’s visit, Myanmar’s military conducted an airstrike on a crowded marketplace in Rakhine state, killing over 50 people and injuring scores more, according to United Nations human rights officials. The State Department said it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests and raises the need to cease violence and release political prisoners. “You don't solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing them,” spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement. A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Min Aung Hlaing, who has cited electoral fraud to justify the coup and labelled his opponents as terrorists, is seeking international legitimacy for his nominally civilian government. Current and former officials say Vance has met players from all sides of Myanmar’s complex conflict and helped shape the Trump administration’s policy toward the country. Intelligence chiefs - such as Vance - do not typically steer policy because of concerns about compromising analytic independence. “If you let policy dictate to intelligence, you can't be sure you're getting a real honest assessment of the facts,” said Richard Betts, an adjunct senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who has consulted for US intelligence agencies. Pigott declined to address Vance’s role but said the administration “operates as a team with the president as the lead”.

Related:

Southeast Asia remains 'a clear priority' despite concerns over Trump tariffs: US envoy to ASEAN

A DETAINED AMERICAN, AND AN OPENING Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained at Yangon airport on Jun 11 by Myanmar authorities on what his supporters have described as trumped-up charges. The US government has not commented on whether Castillo was wrongfully detained. People familiar with the matter said White House, National Security Council and State Department officials held back-channel negotiations with Myanmar officials to secure his release. One person said Myanmar asked only "to have an official engagement at the right level with the US government" in return. Castillo declined to comment beyond crediting President Donald Trump for his release. The meeting builds on a June meeting between US and Myanmar officials in Tokyo also involving Vance, four people said. One of the people said officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part. It was unclear who represented Myanmar at the talks. Vance, who became involved in Myanmar policy while advising Vice President JD Vance on Asian affairs, has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military, five of the people said. A major focus of the US push is getting Myanmar's help in shuttering scam hubs operating on its territory that run romance and other frauds, which have scammed Americans out of billions of dollars. Two people familiar with the matter said the FBI has had direct contact with Myanmar’s authorities on cyber scams. Researchers say many scams are run from areas under militia control, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar’s leaders are serious about enforcement. US officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive deposits of heavy rare earths that are used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. US officials acknowledge obstacles: the deposits mainly lie in territory held by ethnic armies fighting Myanmar’s military government, and China, currently the main importer, could see any US role as a challenge. Still, with Washington seeking to diversify supply chains away from China, Myanmar's deposits remain a recurring topic in conversations, the people said.

ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus

Following a 2021 military coup , the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.  During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar. The five points are: First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint. Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people. Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN. Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre. Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.

Collapse Expand

FROM SANCTIONS TO ENGAGEMENT After the 2021 coup, President Joe Biden's administration froze Myanmar's assets at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and imposed sanctions on senior officers and military‑linked businesses. In 2022, Congress authorised non-lethal support for the opposition, funding early-warning systems for airstrikes and incentives for officers to defect. Most of those programs were cut during Trump’s foreign-aid overhaul last year, according to four current and former officials and State Department correspondence with Congress reviewed by Reuters. The State Department said its engagement with the military government does not diminish its relationships with other groups. The US continues to provide assistance to areas outside military control, it said, without detailing that aid. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said the shift was “contrary to both our values and our interests”. “By engaging Min Aung Hlaing while failing to implement congressionally mandated sanctions and deploy appropriated democracy funding, Secretary (Marco) Rubio is ceding US leadership and providing this murderous regime greater international legitimacy,” Meeks said in a statement to Reuters. Myanmar's government, installed after elections criticised by rights groups as a sham, has hired lobbyists to press its case in Washington. In April, Roger Stone, a longtime Trump adviser, began consulting for DCI Group on behalf of Myanmar's Ministry of Information, according to Foreign Agents Registration Act filings. Stone was convicted in 2019 of obstructing a congressional investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump later pardoned him. A newsletter distributed by DCI warned in June that Washington risked being shut out of access to critical minerals if it did not engage with Myanmar. Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he looks for greater international legitimacy after being installed in April as civilian president.

Source: Reuters/nh

FAST

BENGALURU, Oct 8 : India defended its satellite internet approval process as fair and non-discriminatory on Thursday, hours after billionaire Elon Musk accused unnamed "oligarchs" of blocking Starlink's launch in the South Asian nation. Starlink was being blocked by "certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people," Musk wrote on X, without naming anyone. India's telecom market is dominated by billionaires Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Jio and Sunil Mittal's Bharti Airtel. Their satellite internet ventures, alongside Musk's Starlink, have secured early approvals to launch in India but are awaiting spectrum assignment and final clearances. Airtel and Jio did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The wait has stretched on for four years for Starlink, following scrutiny over security requirements and access to spectrum. Responding to Musk's comments, India's telecommunications ministry said three entities were at broadly the same regulatory stage, with security assessments under way for each. It did not name the companies or Musk. "The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said in a statement. The clash is not new. Musk has previously been at odds with Mittal and Ambani over how India should grant them spectrum, before the three set aside their differences in 2025 to sign separate deals to distribute Starlink devices in India. India offers Starlink, part of Musk's SpaceX, access to a satellite broadband market that Deloitte has forecast will be worth $1.9 billion by 2030. The timing adds a diplomatic layer: the US has pushed Starlink's market access as a goodwill marker in trade talks with tariff-hit countries, and New Delhi and Washington have struggled to finalise a trade deal since reaching a framework in February. Security concerns have also followed the recovery of Starlink equipment in India. Indian authorities have said they found Starlink devices in two separate operations in late 2024: a drug seizure by police in the Andaman and Nicobar islands and an army search in Manipur state. Musk then said Starlink's satellite beams were "turned off over India" and were "never on in the first place", a remark he repeated on Wednesday.

Source: Reuters

BANGKOK, Oct 8 : Thailand's consumer confidence index dropped for the first time in four months in September, hurt by flooding, a slow economic recovery and high living costs, a survey showed on Thursday. • The consumer confidence index of the University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce fell to 52.1 in September from 53.2 in August, it said. • Late last month, Bangkok's governor declared the capital a disaster-affected zone after nearly 300 mm (12 inches) of rain swamped the city in just three days, as much as it typically receives in the whole of September. • Economic damage from the floods is estimated at 22 billion baht to 30 billion baht ($655 million to $893 million), and could remain within that range if conditions start to improve next week, Thanavath Phonvichai, the university's president, told a briefing.

SEOUL: The suspect behind recent cyberattacks targeting South Korea's financial sector may be a 26-year-old based in China's Guangdong province who used a Chinese-developed AI agent tool called ARTEX and Anthropic's ClaudeCode, US cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said. In a report published on Wednesday (Oct 7), CrowdStrike said it uncovered personal details linked to the suspected attacker while analysing AI coding-tool sessions and infrastructure associated with a campaign targeting South Korean financial institutions from late September to early October. The case is likely to intensify concerns over the rise of AI agents and whether organisations are prepared to defend their systems against them. Australia said last month that an OpenAI autonomous agent breached a government health statistics portal in June, marking one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government system.

CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, a recently released Chinese-developed open-source penetration testing tool, alongside large language models such as Claude. "While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated," it said. "This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the use of the Chinese-developed tool ARTEX and observed Chinese-language prompts."

Related:

South Korea's Lee says AI appears to have been used in bank hacks

BANK HACKS CrowdStrike said the individual also asked Claude where threat actors typically sell Korean data breach information and sought assistance in finding Korean Telegram data sales groups. In another session, the person also asked Claude to create a security researcher resume, which included details such as a Telegram account, age, educational background and a location in Maoming, a city in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, which CrowdStrike said likely belonged to the attacker. A man who answered a phone number provided by CrowdStrike in its report said he had no knowledge of the matter. Anthropic, South Korean police and China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ARTEX is an open-source AI agent for automated penetration testing that was published on GitHub this year by a Chinese security engineer with the handle Autumn. It is not a standalone large language model but connects to external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in networks. The tool’s GitHub page says it is intended for personal learning, code research and local technical verification and should not be used to conduct real-world testing against online systems or websites. At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or have been reported by local media as having been targeted by cyberattacks since late September, prompting South Korean police to launch a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures. Shinhan Bank said last week that the personal information of about 25,000 of its customers was compromised, while KB Kookmin Bank said that the personal information of 119 of its customers was leaked.

Source: Reuters/nh

SYDNEY, Oct 8 : Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand. New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.  The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024 with the island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiling the name "Chiefs" the following year.  NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team is officially launched later this month.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR Chief Executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement on Thursday.  "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."  ARLC Executive Chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago. "We will defend this vigorously," he said. "The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval ... "Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games." Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism. While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand. Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.  The new team, which has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands. "We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Lancaster said. "We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

Source: Reuters
